items.name: US Navy wants more visible role for drone boats as one deploys for the first time
items.summary: The U.S. Navy's No. 2 officer shed new light on the value that medium unmanned surface vessels could bring to the fleet.
items.full_text:
While the U.S. Navy has been making significant investments inuncrewed boatsin recent years, key questions have remained about how the service plans toemploy and distributethe new capability.

But in testimony before a congressionally authorized panel earlier this month, the Navy’s No. 2 officer shed new light on the value thatmedium unmanned surface vessels, or MUSVs, could bring to the fleet, particularly as persistently forward-stationed assets and part of tailorable mission packages available to commanders.

Adm. James Kilby, the vice chief of naval operations, cited the recent deployment of an MUSV to the Pacific with the USS Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group — the first operational deployment for the platform — as an example of how the Navy is working to normalize the presence of unmanned assets in operations.

“I see a world where it’s part of your certification exercise,” Kilby told theNational Commission on the Future of the Navyin an Oct. 8 hearing, referring to the proficiency tests Navy ships must complete to demonstrate that they’re qualified for various warfighting operations and mission areas. “You know, there’s elements that we introduce in that exercise where you’ve got to demonstrate that capability, because it’s probably not going to go over with you. You’re going to pick it up over there, and you’ve got to be certified to use it.”

The Navy is expected to receive its firstformal delivery of 30 MUSVsby the end of fiscal 2027. Earlier this month, Navy Secretary Hung Caoconfirmed the deploymentof a drone boat with the Roosevelt Strike Group, calling it a “force multiplier.”

“Imagine having more guns out there,” he said, according to aDefense Scoopreport.

The Navy now operates fourMUSVs, originallybuilt as test bedsand later transferred to the service. Itannounced last monththat it had selected three companies to build a total of 30 of the vessels. The news came about six months after theNavy pivoted on its MUSVprogram to accelerate drone boat development, citing a desire for the vessels to become an integral part of its new “Golden Fleet” concept.

Kilby noted that the Navy had also recently created a Robotic and Autonomous Systems Warfighting Development Center (RASWDC) at Joint Expeditionary Base Little Creek-Fort Story in Virginia Beach, which he said was based on Navy Fighter Weapons School, also known as Top Gun, in Fallon, Nevada.

“The idea, in the case of MUSVs is, the surface community would certify an element to go forward and operate with the fleet. If they work with other [robotic and autonomous systems] entities, the commander of RASWDC will create that total tailored force package,” Kilby said.

“The Secretary of War is developing capability very fast, from an unmanned perspective, and the Navy needs to do a better job of integrating with that capability, so we know what we’re receiving. Because we will have a manning, training and equipping responsibility for those things,” he continued.

He added that he was “not satisfied” with where the Navy was in preparation to receive the soon-to-arrive MUSVs, but believed the service had what it required to “provide the governance and structure you need moving forward.”

The Navy has cited a broad range of potential roles anduses for the MUSV,from reconnaissance and surveillance platforms to controllable weapons carriers, thanks to modular payloads.

Speaking about unmanned systems more generally, Kilby said the Navy, while making progress on training, had ground to cover to make the systems an integrated part of the fleet.

“It is the force development, the employment, the development beyond the [concept of operations] that we need help with,” Kilby said, “And [having] a sustainable plan so that we can bring that force to bear when we need it.”

Hope Hodge Seck is an award-winning investigative and enterprise reporter covering the U.S. military and national defense. The former managing editor of Military.com, her work has also appeared in the Washington Post, Politico Magazine, USA Today and Popular Mechanics.

items.name: US Navy reports highest number of Class A aviation, afloat mishaps in 10 years
items.summary: The U.S. Navy reported a decade-high number of unplanned catastrophic events involving aircraft and vessels.
items.full_text:
The U.S. Navyannouncedthat fiscal 2026 brought the most unplanned catastrophic events involving aircraft and vessels in a decade.

Sixteen Class A aviation and 11 Class A afloat mishaps occurred during that span, according to data released by theNavy Safety Commandand updated Monday.

The Navy defines Class A mishaps as those that cause $2.5 million or more in damage or destruction of an aircraft or lead to fatalities or permanent total disability.

The tally of unplanned aerial and afloat calamities includes several that occurred in the Middle East during the Iran war, which began on Feb. 28 after President Donald Trump launched Operation Epic Fury.

A U.S. Navy aircrewman wentmissingon July 1 after an MH-60S Sea Hawk helicopter, assigned to the USS George H.W. Bush in the Middle East, made an emergency landing in the Arabian Sea.

The missing sailor was later presumed dead. The other three crew members were rescued.

The controlled crash was not a result of any hostilities, and the Navy is investigating the cause of the crash, the service said.

The Navy also dealt with a high-profile fire aboard the world’s largest aircraft carrier.

The USS Gerald R. Fordexperienceda non-combat blaze on March 12 in the main laundry room while it was operating in the Red Sea in support of Operation Epic Fury.

Three sailors were injured, and one was flown off the ship to receive medical treatment.

The fire took over 30 hours to put out anddamagedmore than 600 sailors’ sleeping arrangements, forcing many to sleep on floors and tables. The Ford was forced to leave the theatre for several days to undergo maintenance in Split, Croatia.

Other events occurred away from the fight.

On Sept. 28, six sailors and two aviators wereinjuredafter a landing mishap involving an E/A-18G Growler aboard the Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS Dwight D. Eisenhower. Two pilots were attempting to land the aircraft at 6:18 p.m. off the coast of Virginia when an arresting gear failure forced them to eject from the aircraft.

In anotherincident, an F/A-18F Super Hornet experienced a left engine fire on July 1 while conducting a routine training mission over Naval Air Station Fallon, Nevada.

The crew safely landed the plane with no injuries.

Riley Ceder is a reporter at Military Times, where he covers breaking news, criminal justice, investigations, and cyber. He previously worked as an investigative practicum student at The Washington Post, where he contributed to the Abused by the Badge investigation.
